clinical_category: Joint replacement - individualized home discharge planning
blueprint_topic: Home-environment assessment, caregiver support, equipment planning, and continuity of care
stem: A client preparing for discharge after joint replacement lives alone in a two-story home with loose rugs, no bathroom grab bars, and no available help for the first several days. Which nursing action best supports a safe discharge plan?

options.A: Assess the home and support barriers with the client and interdisciplinary team, arrange needed equipment or assistance, and modify the discharge plan so identified safety needs are addressed before the client is sent home.
options.B: Use the same standard discharge plan as every other joint-replacement client because home layout and caregiver availability do not affect safety.
options.C: Advise the client to leave the rugs and bathroom unchanged because environmental modifications do not influence fall risk during recovery.
options.D: Discharge the client without discussing help at home because social support is unrelated to postoperative self-care and mobility.

rationale: A is correct. AAOS joint-replacement guidance recommends planning the home environment before and after surgery, including secure handrails or grab bars, a stable shower bench or chair, removal of loose rugs and cords, and arranging help with activities during early recovery when needed. AAOS also notes that an alternative discharge setting may be appropriate when the client cannot safely care for themselves at home or lacks needed support. NCSBN places individualized discharge planning, referrals, resource coordination, and continuity of care within Management of Care. B is incorrect because discharge planning should reflect the client's actual functional and environmental circumstances. C contradicts established fall-prevention recommendations. D ignores a major determinant of safe postoperative recovery. The final item is distinct from V2-Q1870: Q1870 tests whether mobility goals have been met, whereas this item tests whether the home environment and support system are adequate.
educational_objective: Individualize joint-replacement discharge planning by assessing the home environment and available support, arranging equipment or services, and resolving fall and self-care barriers before discharge.
source_organization: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Total Knee Replacement; Activities After Total Knee Replacement; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current AAOS OrthoInfo resources accessed 2026-08-18; NCSBN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: AAOS OrthoInfo 'Total Knee Replacement' → Home Planning: secure shower/bath safety bars, stair handrails, stable chair/shower bench, remove loose carpets and cords, and consider a temporary first-floor living space. AAOS 'Activities After Total Knee Replacement' → Recovery at Home/Preparing Your Home: arrange help at home, prepare clear paths for cane/walker/crutches, remove throw rugs and secure cords; if self-care goals/support are inadequate, direct home discharge may be unsafe. NCSBN 2026 Test Plan → Management of Care: discharge planning, referrals, resource use and continuity of care.
source_claim_supported: Current AAOS sources directly support home-safety modifications and planning for assistance after joint replacement; NCSBN supports individualized discharge planning and coordination of necessary resources.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment → Management of Care: develop and update individualized plans of care, coordinate discharge planning, assess referral/resource needs and promote continuity and safety across care settings.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic discharge-planning list into an applied home-environment and support-system scenario. The final item remains Management of Care but is separated from V2-Q1870 by testing environmental/caregiver readiness rather than the client's physical mobility performance.
audit_findings: The source item was a broad list of discharge components and risked semantic overlap with the immediately preceding PT/discharge-readiness item.
Fresh AAOS review directly supports concrete home modifications and arranging assistance during early joint-replacement recovery.
The final construct isolates environmental and support-system readiness rather than repeating physical functional criteria.
Distractors test one-size-fits-all discharge, denial of environmental fall risk and disregard of caregiver availability; none is defensible.

Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct discharge-planning action with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported equipment mandate, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or semantic duplication.
